newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Pakistan to start talks this month - paper.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan to start talks this month - paper.

text.p: An Indian newspaper said on Thursday that India and Pakistan would soon resume talks that broke down three years ago in acrimony.
The Asian Age said Pakistani Foreign Secretary Shamshad Ahmad would meet his Indian counterpart, Salman Haider, in New Delhi for three days of talks starting on March 28. Both are top civil servants.

Haider, reached by telephone at his residence in the Indian capital, declined to comment on the report, which was based on an interview with Pakistan's outgoing high commissioner (ambassador) to India, Riaz Hussain Khokhar.

Khokhar, on his way to Washington for a new posting as ambassador, could not be reached for comment on Thursday. A spokesman for Pakistan's foreign office in Islamabad refused to confirm or deny the report.

Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, speaking to reporters in Mauritius, said the dates of the meeting between the foreign secretaries would be established in the next few days, the Press Trust of India (PTI) said.
The last round of bilateral talks between the South Asian neighbours was held in January 1994 and bogged down in differences over the Himalayan region of Kashmir.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars, two of them over Kashmir, since they gained independence from Britain in 1947.

New Delhi accuses Islamabad of arming and training separatist guerrillas fighting Indian rule in Jammu and Kashmir state, where police and hospital officials say more than 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence since 1990.
Pakistan says it provides only moral and diplomatic support.
Following Nawaz Sharif's election as Pakistan's prime minister last month, India and Pakistan have exchanged letters expressing a desire to resume bilateral talks.
Pakistan said on Saturday that it hoped for an early resumption of talks and was willing to discuss a troop pullout from the disputed Himalayan glacier, Siachen.
Gujral wrote to his Pakistani counterpart, Gohar Ayub Khan, at the weekend, welcoming Pakistan's suggestion that foreign secretaries from the two countries should meet in March.
Pakistan has insisted that the two sides discuss Kashmir. India has said it is keen to narrow differences over less contentious issues to help improve the overall climate between the longtime foes.
"There is no question of any pre-conditions," PTI quoted Gujral as saying on Thursday in Mauritius, where he was attending a meeting of foreign ministers from nations ringing the Indian Ocean.
"They (Pakistan) have not stipulated any pre-condition, and we are not ready to accept any."
Sharif had earlier said that the "core issue" of Kashmir would have to be discussed. "We are ready to discuss all subjects," Gujral was quoted as saying.
